claim: Exclude active subscribers from regular campaigns and sales: one 8-figure brand's campaigns caused more subscription cancels than starts; segmenting helped cut churn from about 19% to 13-14%.
body: An 8-figure brand sent its regular campaigns to non-buyers and active subscribers alike. Tracking the Recharge subscription cancelled event against each campaign showed about 9,400 cancels from campaign recipients, more than the subscriptions those campaigns started, so the campaign programme was net negative for subscriptions. After excluding active subscribers, cancels attributed to campaigns dropped to near zero, worth about $24k a month in net improvement, and together with other changes monthly churn fell from roughly 19% to 13-14%. Every send reminds a subscriber they could reconsider, and a sitewide sale tempts them to cancel and rebuy cheaper. The rule: send active subscribers 1 to 3 deliberate campaigns a month (a founder newsletter, community news, a subscriber-only giveaway), always exclude them from sale campaigns, and give them their own sale mechanic instead, such as a discount on a one-time add-on to their next order (for example 30% off protein added to a creatine subscription). How to apply: build an active-subscriber segment from the subscription app's profile properties, exclude it from every campaign by default, and measure subscription cancelled within a few days of each send.
conditions: Subscription brands with a meaningful share of revenue from active subscribers and an ESP synced with subscription status.
fails_when: Brands with tiny subscriber bases where exclusion adds complexity without effect; ghosting subscribers entirely also hurts (both this speaker and Matt Holman warn against silence).

claim: In one 8-figure brand, the biggest churn spike was day 30, the first rebill, triggered by the plain Shopify order confirmation, about double the spike from the billing reminder.
body: Plotting cancels by days since subscription start for an 8-figure subscription brand showed: a small spike at day 0, near zero until delivery, a bump after first use, a bump at the billing reminder, and the largest spike at day 30, when the first renewal charged and Shopify sent its default receipt (you were just charged this amount, view your order). That receipt produced roughly twice the cancels of the billing reminder that preceded it. Many teams optimise billing reminders but leave the order confirmation untouched. Fix: replace the default confirmation with a branded transactional email in your ESP, varied by subscription versus one-time order and by renewal number, that leads with the benefit and consistency message, dynamic order contents, testimonials and any gift included in this order. How to apply: chart cancels by day since start from your subscription app to find your own spikes, then target the emails that sit on them. Switching off Shopify's native confirmation depends on your plan and Shopify support; the speaker's description of which plan allows it is unclear, so check Shopify's current notification settings before removing it, and keep a legally adequate receipt either way.
conditions: Shopify stores with a subscription app sending default Shopify order confirmations on renewals.
fails_when: Brands that already send customised renewal confirmations; jurisdictions or plan settings that require Shopify's own receipt to stay on. One brand's curve; yours may peak elsewhere.

claim: Rebuilding the subscription billing reminder in Klaviyo (benefits first, delay button high, manage-subscription link at the bottom) cut cancels from that email from 8.6% to 5.8%.
body: Billing reminders are legally required in some US states before a recurring charge and should not be skipped, but the default reminder from the subscription app (Recharge, Skio) is stark: the charge amount and a big manage subscription button, which invites the customer to reconsider. In an A/B test the agency moved the reminder into Klaviyo and redesigned it, reducing the cancel rate on that email from 8.6% to 5.8%, about a third fewer cancels, which they valued at tens of thousands of dollars a month for that brand. The structure: an upbeat headline about the next order and the habit being built; the perks (discount level, free gifts in the coming order, pause or skip anytime); a one-click delay link near the top, because too much product is the top cancel reason; upsell and cross-sell blocks; and only at the very bottom a manage subscription link. Then build a separate version per rebill number (first, second, third renewal) and per product, and when a gift is due in the next order, make the gift the headline. How to apply: switch off the app's native reminder, rebuild it as a Klaviyo flow on the upcoming-charge event, and keep a clear cancel path to stay compliant.
conditions: Subscription brands on Recharge, Skio or similar with Klaviyo; US state auto-renewal laws apply to reminder content and timing.
fails_when: Hiding or obstructing cancellation can breach auto-renewal and click-to-cancel rules; the cancel path must stay clear and the required disclosures present. A single-brand test; lift will vary.

claim: Send daily onboarding emails in the 7 days before delivery, when almost nobody cancels, then go quiet during days 7 to 14 when cancels spike after receipt.
body: The speaker describes the cancel curve he sees across subscription accounts: a spike on day 0 from people who only wanted the deal, close to zero cancels between purchase and delivery (roughly days 2 to 7, because nobody judges a product they have not tried), then a second spike around delivery and first use, roughly days 7 to 14. Every email is a reminder that cancelling is possible, so the sending should be concentrated where it is safe. Plan: a founder thank-you immediately; daily (minimum every other day) education emails before the product lands, covering what it is, why it works, how and when to use it; a delivery-day message with quick usage tips; perhaps one check-in at week one or two; then back off and let the customer experience the product. SMS follows the same plan at every other day rather than daily. Upcoming gift reminders move into billing reminders and order confirmations rather than extra campaigns. How to apply: pull days-until-cancel for your subscribers (Klaviyo or the subscription app) to confirm your own curve before copying the timing, since shipping times change where the safe window falls.

claim: Survey subscribers on when they take the product, find the routine with the highest retention (creatine in morning coffee), then make onboarding push that one habit.
body: A creatine brand had many cancels for too much product. A survey asked how customers take their creatine each day; answers included before the gym, before brushing teeth at night, with breakfast and in morning coffee. Cutting retention and LTV by answer showed the coffee group retained significantly better, because coffee happens every morning and the creatine sits next to it, so doses are not forgotten. This is habit stacking: attach the product to an existing daily trigger. The brand then rewrote onboarding to repeat one instruction, put it in your coffee, and LTV rose (no exact figure given). How to apply: add a post-purchase or day-14 survey question about when and with what the customer uses the product; store the answer as a profile property; after 60 to 90 days compare retention by answer; pick the routine with the best retention that most people could adopt; make it the hero instruction in onboarding emails, inserts and the product page. Also tell customers the realistic time to results (the speaker uses 90 to 120 days for daily supplements) so they do not judge it too early. Repeat the instruction across several emails; people need reminding more than teaching.
conditions: Daily-use consumables where missed doses drive overstock and cancels; enough subscribers to compare cohorts by survey answer.
fails_when: Small samples (a few dozen responses per answer) make the retention difference noise; products whose use is tied to a fixed event already (pre-workout) gain less.

claim: Win back cancelled subscribers 30 to 60 days after cancelling with a deeper first-reorder offer (30 to 50% off, then back to standard 15%), not immediately.
body: Right after cancelling, a subscriber has just declined every save offer in the portal, so an immediate email rarely brings them back; the speaker keeps the post-cancel flow to one or two simple emails confirming the cancel, acknowledging the reason and showing a reactivate button. The cancelled customer then returns to the normal campaign cadence, where some come back on their own. For those who still have not bought, a subscriber win-back flow starts 30 to 60 days after cancellation and is where offers get tested: for example 30%, 40% or 50% off the first resubscribed order, dropping to the standard 15% recurring discount afterwards. Link straight to the portal's resubscribe action so it takes one click, restate the perks, and show the founders' faces for a personal note. He suggests segmenting the win-back by cancel reason; Matt Holman, a subscription agency founder, argues the opposite, that testing one strong offer for everyone gives faster, more conclusive reads. How to apply: set the delay, test two offer depths, and track reactivation rate and the retention of reactivated subscribers, since deep discounts can bring back customers who churn again.
conditions: Subscription brands with enough monthly cancels to test win-back offers; margin room for one deeply discounted order.
fails_when: Thin-margin products where a 40-50% reorder loses money if the customer churns again; products whose cancel reason is product dislike, where no discount brings them back.

claim: Brands doing a few million a year in subscription revenue typically lose 5-10% of it to failed payments and weak dunning; segment dunning flows by payment method.
body: Holman says every subscription app claims to handle failed-payment recovery best, but a brand with a few million dollars of annual subscription revenue is probably losing 5 to 10% of it to bad processing and dunning. Third-party recovery tools such as Churn Buster and FlyCode (the transcript garbles a third name), along with better emails, recover part of this. The tactic he runs on Skio: segment failed-payment flows by payment type, because the fix differs. PayPal failures get a PayPal-specific flow, Shop Pay failures a Shop Pay flow, card failures a card update flow, with card reactivation as the fallback in each. Let the platform's retry logic run first; once the order hits a failure state, start email and SMS and be aggressive, since there is nothing to lose: the order is not processing, so the customer will either update payment, cancel, or lapse. SMS is singled out as well suited here. How to apply: pull failed-charge counts and recovered amounts from the subscription app for the last 90 days, size the loss against subscription revenue, then build method-specific flows and consider a specialist tool if the loss is above about 5%.
conditions: Subscription brands with recurring card, PayPal and Shop Pay charges; platforms that expose payment-failure type (Skio named).
fails_when: Platforms that do not pass the failure type to the ESP; very small subscription revenue where a specialist tool costs more than it recovers.

claim: For subscription win-back, test one aggressive offer for all cancelled subscribers weekly rather than splitting flows by cancel reason; more volume gives conclusive reads faster.
body: Segmenting win-back emails by cancellation reason was a popular approach, and the companion WellCopy video still recommends it. Holman has moved away from it: if the offer is good, the cancel reason matters less, and splitting a modest list into five or seven reason-based flows leaves each with too few sends to tell which offer works. He would rather test effective win-back offers for everyone every week or two and read click and reactivation rates. Offers he likes cross the catalog: 50% off if you come back and buy product A and B together, or free product B for three months when you resubscribe to three months of product A. He keeps offers out of the cancel confirmation email, reasoning that if a better offer existed it should have been used in the cancel flow; the confirmation should instead set the stage for return, for example reminding supplement users that results take sustained use and inviting them back. Segment by reason only if you have the bandwidth. How to apply: run a single win-back flow, rotate one offer variable per test window, and judge on reactivation and the second-cycle retention of those reactivated.
conditions: Subscription brands with moderate cancel volumes and a catalog of two or more SKUs for cross-product offers.
fails_when: Very large brands with enough volume per reason to test reason-specific flows; cancels driven by product dislike, where an offer for the same product will not convert.

claim: Shopify Messaging's abandoned-cart automation skips anyone sent a cart, checkout or browse email in the last 14 days; full sender-domain authentication takes up to 48 hours.
body: Two mechanics from Shopify's own walkthrough of Shopify Messaging. First, abandoned checkout recovery is already on by default under Marketing, Automations, and sends a few hours after abandonment with a one-click link back to the cart. The separate abandoned cart automation (someone added at least one item but never started checkout) must be turned on; it automatically excludes anyone who already received an abandoned checkout, abandoned cart or browse email in the last 14 days, so stacking these flows does not spam the same person. Plan sequences around that window rather than adding a second tool that ignores it. Second, sender setup: you can verify the sender address quickly with a verification email and start sending at once, or authenticate the domain by adding DNS records, which is better for long-term inbox placement and can take up to 48 hours to take effect. The tutorial recommends quick verification to start and domain authentication soon after. Use a branded address such as hello@yourdomain rather than a free mailbox.

claim: For a time-limited launch, send 10 new emails, resend each to non-openers with a new subject line, and send three closing emails on the final day.
body: Jamie's launch structure for promotions with a hard deadline. Volume: 10 new emails, each resent to unopens with a different subject line (and ideally new preview text), so about 20 sends. Cadence options: aggressive, about 10 days, alternating each morning's resend of yesterday's email with an evening new email; moderate, about 20 days with a breather between; relaxed, longer. She mostly uses aggressive or moderate and reports little revenue difference between them; large lists (hundreds of thousands of contacts) gain most from resends because thousands still have not seen email one. Content: email 1 is 'Introducing: [product name]', a hard sell; expect opens about half your usual rate (around 15% against a normal 25 to 30%), but openers are the most interested. Emails 2 to 7 mix quick-win lessons with a product reminder, repurposed content, testimonials and an FAQ email built from real questions. Emails 8 to 10 are the triple close, all sent on the last day (morning, afternoon, evening). She says adding the triple close doubled launch revenue for a client compared with earlier launches and has used it on every launch since, but gives no sample size or list data. The talk is undated; open rates now include Apple Mail Privacy Protection auto-opens, so compare against your own baseline.

claim: Count as engaged: a non-Apple-privacy open or non-bot click within 180 days, or sign-up or site visit within 14 days; sunset after 180 days of no opens or clicks.
body: Since iOS 15, Apple Mail Privacy Protection loads emails automatically, so raw opens overstate engagement, and bots also click links. Dispatch's engaged segment in Klaviyo counts someone as engaged if they opened an email in the last 180 days where the open was not an Apple privacy open, or clicked in the last 180 days where the click was not a bot click, or subscribed in the last 14 days (they have only had one or two emails so far), or were active on site in the last 14 days (fresh intent, like ad retargeting). The profile must still be able to receive email. Split it into prospects (zero orders) and customers (at least one order), each with 90, 180 and 365-day versions. Send everyday and evergreen campaigns to the 90-day engaged group, and widen to the 365-day group only for big moments such as Black Friday or major launches. Do not slice campaign audiences into very small segments. For list hygiene, a sunset flow triggers when someone has zero opens and zero clicks in 180 days, sends about three last-chance emails with a strong offer (a unique code so it cannot leak), says in the last email that they will be removed, then suppresses anyone still unengaged.
conditions: Klaviyo accounts (or ESPs that flag Apple privacy opens and bot clicks) with lists large enough to segment; most ecommerce brands.
fails_when: Very long purchase cycles (furniture, annual purchases) where 180 days of silence is normal; there use longer windows. Tiny lists where a 90-day segment is too small to send to.

claim: In abandoned checkout flows send email and SMS together rather than SMS then email hours later, test shorter delays (2h vs Klaviyo's 4h), and branch prospects from returning customers.
body: Klaviyo's abandoned checkout template waits four hours and then sends SMS to people who can receive it, otherwise email. Dispatch changes three things. First, delay: shorter delays usually convert better, so they A/B test the four-hour default against two hours for every client, using a random 50% conditional split before the delay. Second, channel: instead of SMS for some and email for others, they send email and SMS at the same time or close together, because you cannot know which channel will convert a given person, and the either-or setup can leave someone waiting about 20 hours for the email when every hour counts. Third, audience: split by 'placed order at least once'. Prospects get a reminder of their welcome offer, the exact cart contents, unique selling points, and in later emails one or two of the most common objections (price, value, proof via specific reviews), with at least three emails; a second email about 20 hours later is a starting point. Returning customers are not eligible for the welcome offer, so use subscription, loyalty or other repeat incentives and address returning-buyer objections. Browse abandonment uses the same split with 2 versus 4-hour tests. Avoid fixed send times such as 9 a.m. in these flows.

fails_when: Markets with strict SMS rules or quiet hours (send times must respect them); brands without SMS consent; very high-ticket purchases where a slower, more considered sequence fits.

claim: Klaviyo defaults to 5-day open and 5-day click attribution; shorten it (e.g. 3 days) for impulse products, and exclude transactional emails, bot clicks and Apple privacy opens.
body: Klaviyo credits a purchase to the last email a person opened or clicked within its attribution window, which defaults to five days for opens and five for clicks. That inflates email revenue for impulse purchases, where the email five days earlier probably did not cause the order. Dispatch shortens the window for impulse categories, for example to three days for both, and keeps or lengthens it only for long-consideration products such as $10,000 furniture, where a nurture email from weeks earlier may truly have contributed. They advise not straying far from five and five as a conservative default. In the same settings, exclude transactional messages (order confirmations) from attribution, exclude bot clicks on email and SMS, and exclude Apple Mail Privacy Protection opens, which are automatic since iOS 15 and would otherwise credit emails nobody read. Set smart sending (Klaviyo default 16 hours) so a person does not get several marketing emails in a short window. How to apply: set these before judging flows or campaigns, note the change date, and compare email-attributed revenue with total store revenue rather than reading Klaviyo's figure as incremental. The presenter's target is email at 30% or more of total store revenue, a practitioner benchmark.
conditions: Brands using Klaviyo attribution to judge email performance; impulse versus considered purchase decides window length.
fails_when: Treating any window as incrementality; attribution windows only change what is credited, so holdout tests are needed to know what email really adds.

claim: Raise sends from 1 to 4 a week while click rate, unsubscribes and complaints hold, judging by unique clicks; opens under 30% or clicks under 0.5% flag deliverability trouble.
body: More sends lower open and click rates almost by definition, which scares brands away from sending more. Dispatch judges frequency by unique counts instead. In one client example, open rate fell while unique opens rose about 40%; with click rate down only about 10%, total unique clicks rose sharply, so more people were reached and revenue grew. Their test: move from one to four campaigns a week and watch click-through rate, unsubscribe rate and spam complaint rate. If those stay roughly flat, the list is telling you it wants more email and you should keep the higher cadence. If they jump, back off. Commit only to a cadence the team can sustain; a steady two a week beats four one week and one the next, because consistency itself supports sender reputation alongside SPF, DKIM and DMARC. The presenter avoids hard benchmarks but gives two floors: campaign open rate should be above 30% and click rate above 0.5%; below either, assume a deliverability problem before blaming content. Read open rate as subject line, targeting and timing; click rate as interest in the content and offer; placed-order rate as the offer and site.

fails_when: Small or very cold lists where higher frequency quickly raises complaints; open-rate floors are unreliable where privacy opens are excluded or ESP reporting differs.

claim: Target popup sign-up above 9% of traffic (Klaviyo badges 3% as excellent) with a 4-step form: yes/no offer step, email, SMS, then success page.
body: Dispatch, an email agency that says it has A/B tested hundreds of popup forms, holds client popups to converting more than 9% of site traffic, and calls Klaviyo's 'excellent' badge at 3% too low a bar. Their form structure has four steps. Step one is a micro-commitment: show the offer and ask only yes or no ('Claim 20% off' or 'I'm not interested'), with no email field yet; having said yes, many more people complete step two. Step two collects the email. Step three asks for the phone number for SMS on a separate SMS list, even if SMS flows are not built yet. Step four confirms success and, ideally, says the code was sent to their inbox and phone, so the first email is opened and clicked, which helps sender reputation. Settings that won their tests: popup format over flyout or full page; turn off 'click outside to close' so a stray tap does not dismiss it; load immediately rather than after a delay; no image, so attention goes to the offer; a teaser tab that reopens the form after closing; show to all visitors who are not subscribed; and design and test mobile separately, since most visitors are on mobile.

fails_when: Brands that avoid discounts or popups for positioning reasons, or where an immediate full popup harms search rankings or mobile experience; B2B or very high-ticket stores where visitors are not deal-motivated.

claim: Send 3-4 campaigns a week to the engaged list; an agency testing 200+ brands found 1-2 under-earns and 5-7 raises unsubscribes and plateaus.
body: An email agency claiming over $200 million in attributed email revenue says its cadence tests across more than 200 brands point to 3 to 4 campaigns per week to engaged subscribers. Below that, new subscribers forget the brand before they decide, never form a habit of opening, and senders build less positive reputation with Gmail, so inbox placement suffers. At 5 to 7 a week, unsubscribes climb, messages dilute each other and revenue stops rising. Four sends a week is about 16 a month, which needs a content plan, not just promotions. How to apply: 1) define the engaged segment (recent openers or clickers, recent buyers) and send the higher cadence only there; 2) step up from your current frequency one send at a time; 3) watch unsubscribe and spam-complaint rates per send and revenue per recipient across the month, not per email; 4) keep the less engaged on a lower cadence or sunset them. claim: An SMS segment holds 160 standard characters; one character over bills two, a single emoji drops the limit to 70, and MMS costs 2 to 3x SMS.
body: SMS is billed per segment, so length decisions are cost decisions. A message in the standard GSM-7 character set fits 160 characters in one segment; at 161 it becomes a multi-part message billed as two (each part then holds slightly fewer characters because of joining data), and so on. The source warns that emojis 'eat 35 to 50 characters'; the actual mechanism is that any emoji or non-GSM character switches the whole message to Unicode (UCS-2) encoding, where one segment holds only 70 characters, so a 100-character text with one emoji costs two segments. MMS (image or GIF) messages typically cost two to three times an SMS, so the image must lift revenue by the same multiple to pay back, which the operator, who reports sending tens of millions of messages, says is very rare. How to apply: write SMS as text-only, plain characters, under 160 including the link and opt-out language; check the platform's segment counter before sending; reserve MMS for sends where a visual is the offer (a product drop) and test MMS against SMS on revenue per recipient; avoid smart quotes and special symbols pasted from documents, which also trigger Unicode encoding.

fails_when: Plans billed per message rather than per segment; markets or carriers with different pricing; brands where an image genuinely drives much higher revenue (visual product launches) as shown by a test.

claim: The first send to a list that has been silent for months will spike unsubscribes (Hormozi: just over 1%) before settling (his list: 0.42% per email); send anyway.
body: Unsubscribes are pulled-forward churn. When a list has not been emailed for months, the first send collects the opt-outs that would have trickled out over the silent period, so the rate spikes once and then falls. Hormozi's own numbers: his first-ever email to his list unsubscribed just over 1%; a steady cadence later ran at about 0.42% per email, with an open rate of 35.7% (he distrusts this figure after Apple's privacy change) and click-through of about 8.5% of all recipients over a 90-day period of nearly 10 million sends. His rule: unsubscribes are acceptable as long as the list grows faster between sends than it shrinks. Make unsubscribing easy, because people who cannot leave go dormant instead, and dormant recipients drag down engagement signals and inbox placement for everyone. Practical steps for a store restarting email: expect a one-time spike on the first one or two sends, do not read it as a content failure, suppress long-term non-openers or run a re-engagement send first, then hold a regular cadence so churn does not build up again. Judge emails on clicks (as a share of all recipients and of openers) rather than opens.
conditions: Lists that have been dormant for months and are being restarted; list sizes large enough that rates are stable.
fails_when: The list was bought, scraped or never opted in, where a spike signals spam complaints and can damage the sending domain; or unsubscribes stay above the restart level after several sends, which signals a content or frequency problem rather than pulled-forward churn.

claim: Pick email reviews to answer one known objection each (taste, ease of swallowing, lab testing, results timing), not generic 'I love it' praise.
body: The agency owner's point is that most brands drop a top-rated generic review into emails, which helps no one decide. Mechanism: a review that names the exact worry a reader has (bitter taste, hard to swallow, hidden lead content, no energy change, thinning hair) answers that objection in a customer's voice, which reads as more credible than brand copy. How to apply: 1) Build an objection list from recent (not top) Amazon reviews of competitor products, Trustpilot, ad comment threads and podcast comments; spend roughly 30 to 60 minutes per product. 2) Tag your own reviews by the objection they answer. 3) In each email, choose two or three reviews that match the email's angle, for example one on hair and nails and one on energy for a busy founder without lifestyle change. 4) Add the reviewer's photo when it builds trust, but omit faces next to sensitive problems (sexual health, skin conditions) for privacy. 5) Rotate review blocks by segment once you know which objection each segment holds. Related layout rules from the same module: keep the banner's purpose readable without scrolling on mobile, and avoid 3 by 2 product grids on mobile; use one product per row with copy, or a 2 by 2 grid with titles only.
conditions: DTC brands with enough reviews to tag by objection; problem-solution and consumable products where objections are specific.
fails_when: Brands with very few reviews, where cherry-picking makes emails look thin or staged; or regulated categories where a review making a health claim would be treated as the brand's own claim.

avoid 3x2 product grids on mobile; use 1 per row or 2x2

claim: About 25% of double-opt-in SMS subscribers buy within 30 days, so treat the pop-up and SMS welcome as part of acquisition, owned jointly with paid media.
body: Across roughly 20,000 to 25,000 Shopify brands on Postscript, about 20 to 27% (usually quoted as 25%) of people who give a phone number through a compliant double opt-in buy something within 30 days. That makes SMS look like a retention channel, but it means the welcome flow is converting people who clicked a paid ad yesterday and did not buy: the pop-up is effectively the first thing that happens after a paid click, and the remaining 75% are prospects with an unresolved objection. Practical consequences discussed: the performance team should know what the pop-up and welcome flow look like; pop-up changes should be tested against full-site conversion rate, because a form that grows the list can hurt purchases; and ad changes can hit list growth (one brand saw SMS subscriber growth fall below forecast after switching ads to view optimisation). Grüns' 23 pre-purchase messages are an acquisition tactic, not retention. For brands at $5 to $10 million a year, the first priority is list growth through the pop-up, then frequency, then conversation. How to apply: report SMS welcome revenue alongside paid acquisition, review pop-up acquisition rate weekly, and put pop-up, welcome flow and media under one growth owner or shared reporting.

fails_when: Brands where most subscribers are existing customers (post-purchase opt-ins), for whom SMS really is retention; the 25% figure is the vendor's cross-brand average and varies widely by category and price.

claim: End an SMS flow message with a simple question ('anything I can help with?'); brands get thousands of replies, and subscribers who converse show about 1.5x subscriber LTV.
body: Postscript started by having about 50 people text shoppers by hand on brands' behalf to learn why subscribers stayed on lists for a year without buying, then built that into an AI agent. The cheapest way to start, without any tool, is to add a question to an existing automated text, such as the last welcome message or the cart reminder: is there anything else I can help you with today? Mannheimer says brands at $500 million a year doubted customers would reply, then received around 5,000 replies in the first week. Replies surface objections no product page can carry: a buyer who gardens five hours a day in the sun and needs to know if a balm survives sweat; a buyer $7 short of their budget who would convert with a small concession; a wife describing her husband's 40-pound weight loss to buy a new belt size. Postscript reports that subscribers who have a conversation with a brand have about 1.5 times higher subscriber LTV, though that is correlational because engaged people reply. Ridge split-tested a six-message welcome flow against the same flow ending in a question. Conversation-first works best for long consideration, high-ticket items and one-time to subscription upsells. How to apply: add the question, staff or automate replies within hours, and tag recurring objections back into page copy and flows.
conditions: Brands with SMS lists and capacity (human or AI) to answer replies quickly; strongest for high-consideration or personalised products (shade matching, furniture).
fails_when: No one answers replies promptly, which damages trust; impulse products with short decision cycles gain little; the 1.5x LTV figure is vendor data and correlational.

claim: Postscript data shows 8-10 SMS per subscriber per month with no rise in first-30-day unsubscribes; a holdout found doubling from one to two texts weekly significantly lifted revenue.
body: Mike Mannheimer of Postscript, an SMS platform, says its subscriber LTV benchmark balances list acquisition rate, messages per subscriber per month, revenue per message and unsubscribe rate, and that the sweet spot across its brands is about 8 to 10 texts per subscriber per month with essentially no change in the unsubscribe rate measured over the first 30 days. Some large brands send about two a month; Grüns sends around 23 messages in a subscriber's first 30 days. An incrementality test with Jones Road split SMS subscribers 50% normal cadence, 25% no messages (holdout) and 25% double cadence (one to two campaigns a week); the double group produced significantly more revenue against the holdout at about 98% certainty, and higher ROI. Because every text costs money, unlike email, frequency should be set by testing: add one message a week (or every two weeks), watch unsubscribe rate and revenue per message, and keep stepping up until unsubscribes tick up; that point is the new baseline. As SMS bills reach $10k to $100k a month, run holdouts to prove incrementality rather than trusting attributed revenue. Treat the vendor's numbers as directional: the speaker benefits when brands send more.
conditions: US SMS programmes with double opt-in lists and per-message costs; brands with enough subscribers to run a holdout split.
fails_when: Low-margin products where per-message cost exceeds incremental revenue; large lists of long-tenure non-buyers, where extra sends mostly add fees (the Grüns example deliberately limits spend on people unlikely to subscribe); TCPA quiet hours and consent rules still apply.

claim: RCS messaging (carousels, video, add-to-calendar buttons, SMS fallback) is live on US devices and outperforming SMS/MMS for early adopters, but costs more per message; launch with a holdout.
body: RCS is a separate messaging protocol from SMS: when a recipient's device cannot receive RCS, the platform falls back to SMS. Per Postscript's chief customer officer, it is available on all US devices and dozens of its brands were live at recording. It lifts the creative floor from text (SMS) and single images (MMS) to swipeable carousels, video, in-thread web views and action buttons, including an iOS add-to-calendar button for product drops, so a launch reminder can be saved to the calendar instead of saying watch this space. Early results show outsized performance versus SMS and MMS, partly from standing out in an inbox where few brands use it yet, an advantage that will fade as adoption grows. The risk is cost: carriers charge more, so if lift does not hold, the economics may not justify it. Jones Road went live with a holdout group to measure incrementality. How to apply: ask your SMS provider whether RCS is enabled and priced, start with drops and recommendation carousels where rich media matters, run a holdout from day one, and compare revenue per message net of the higher cost. Expect the speaker's prediction (most 8 to 9 figure brands on RCS within a year) to be vendor optimism until your test confirms it.
conditions: US SMS programmes on providers supporting RCS; time-sensitive (2026 early-adoption window).
fails_when: If the per-message premium outweighs the lift once the novelty fades; markets or devices with low RCS support fall back to SMS and gain nothing.

claim: Collect SMS as step two of the email popup with the same offer ('finish signing up with text to activate 20% off'), not a smaller extra SMS discount.
body: Many brands offer, say, 15% for email and an extra 5% for adding a phone number. This agency prefers to put the best offer on the first step, because a bigger headline offer lifts email sign-ups, and then frame the SMS step as completing that same offer: the email step says 'you've got 20% off', the SMS step says 'finish signing up with text to activate 20% off'. They report this wording tested well across many accounts. Keep each step to one field (email, then phone) rather than one long form. List size still matters after sign-up: in their example, doubling an SMS list from 5,000 to 10,000 people took orders from about 100 to 160 to 180 a month with the same campaigns, so growth has diminishing but real returns. For flows, they state that only one SMS is allowed in most automated flows (abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, browse abandonment), with the welcome flow allowed two, the second 2 to 3 days later as an offer reminder, while email carries the rest of each sequence. Confirm that limit against your SMS platform's and carrier rules, since it is the practitioner's statement, not a cited regulation. Only text explicitly SMS-opted-in contacts, and respect quiet hours (no sends before 8am or after 9pm recipient time; some US states are stricter).
conditions: US ecommerce brands using a combined email and SMS popup and flows (Klaviyo, Attentive, Postscript).
fails_when: The brand's margins cannot carry the full discount on both channels, or SMS opt-in quality matters more than volume (activation-gated offers can attract discount-only sign-ups); jurisdictions with different consent or quiet-hour rules.

claim: Ecommerce SMS: about one campaign a week (two for brands over 8 figures), click rate 5-15%, unsubscribes under 1%, and SMS around 5-15% of total sales.
body: An agency running SMS for ecommerce clients sets these working numbers. Frequency: one SMS campaign a week is the sweet spot; brands above about $10M a year can test two; more than two a week raises unsubscribes with diminishing returns. Purchase cycle matters: a fashion brand bought quarterly can sustain more than a furniture brand bought every 18 months. Content: only direct, click-worthy reasons (sale, early access, restock, back in stock, launch, flash sale); vague nurture or information texts drive unsubscribes. Timing: late morning to early afternoon, roughly 11am to 3pm; when pairing with an email campaign, send the SMS about 5 to 6 hours after the email so the buyer sees the message on two devices. KPIs: ignore SMS open rates; target click rate of at least 5%, up to 15%; unsubscribe rate under 1% per send (under 0.5% is excellent) and slow down above 1%; delivery rate above 90% (95% excellent). Fixes: low clicks, tighten to an engaged segment and make the message more direct; high unsubscribes, send less and drop informational texts. Channel share: done well, SMS should account for at least 5 to 15% of a brand's total sales.
conditions: DTC ecommerce brands in the US running SMS alongside email; frequency guidance scaled by purchase cycle and revenue band.
fails_when: Long-purchase-cycle or high-ticket categories (furniture), where weekly texts will mostly drive opt-outs; markets outside the US with different consent rules; brands where SMS consent was gathered loosely, inflating complaint risk.

claim: A well-set email popup should capture 8 to 12% of site visitors versus a typical 2 to 4%: email only, OR-logic triggers (about 6 seconds, 60% scroll, or exit).
body: The agency's benchmark is that most stores capture 2 to 4 of every 100 visitors into email, and a properly configured popup gets 8 to 12%. Settings it uses in Klaviyo: 1) Build separate mobile and desktop forms. 2) Show the form when any condition is met (exit intent OR a delay OR scroll depth), not only when all are met; requiring all conditions shows it to a tiny audience, so the submit rate looks high but total sign-ups fall. 3) Time delay between 4 and 10 seconds (6 used in the demo), scroll trigger around 50 to 60% (test 40 to 80%). 4) After a close, show again after 3 to 5 days; never re-show after submit. 5) Ask only for email in step one; collect name, birthday or phone in later steps. 6) Add a 'micro-yes' step before the email field ('Do you want 10% off your first order?' with a yes button). 7) Make the form large and the button contrasting. 8) Add a teaser tab before and after the form. 9) Use single opt-in and clean unengaged profiles later through segments. 10) Judge tests on total sign-ups, not submit rate, because a shorter delay lowers rate but can raise volume. The offer is the biggest lever on sign-up rate.
conditions: Shopify stores using Klaviyo (or a similar form tool) with paid or organic traffic; consumer DTC brands.
fails_when: Markets where single opt-in is not allowed or double opt-in is expected (e.g. Germany), luxury brands where an intrusive popup harms positioning, or Google mobile intrusive-interstitial concerns on SEO-heavy landing pages.

claim: Campaigns per week: about 2 to 3 under 50k monthly revenue, 3 to 4 above 50k, 4 to 5 above 200k; add sends only while opens exceed 30%.
body: The agency's cadence guideline, with a gate: frequency follows revenue band but is only raised when list health supports it. Rule: if you send one campaign a week with open rate above 30% and low unsubscribes, move to two; repeat. If you send four a week with open rate below 30% and rising unsubscribes, do not add more even above 200k a month; clean the list first. Rarely exceed five a week unless segmentation means each person still receives about three. Discount discipline: at least a 5:1 ratio of non-discount to discount campaigns, and the agency prefers 10:1, which works out to about one discount email a month outside Q4; some clients go two months with none. Fill the calendar from content buckets (product highlight, value or educational, social proof, brand values, national days, promotions) and avoid two salesy emails back to back. Note that open rate is inflated by Apple Mail privacy opens, so read it from a source that excludes them. Sends in the demo calendar: Tuesday, Thursday, Sunday.
conditions: DTC brands with an engaged list sending campaigns from Klaviyo; revenue bands are monthly total store revenue.
fails_when: Small or newly built lists where 3 to 4 sends a week burn through engaged subscribers; brands in categories with infrequent purchase (furniture, mattresses) where weekly sends drive unsubscribes; open-rate gates distorted by Apple privacy opens.

claim: Define unengaged as zero opens and clicks and no site activity in 120 days after at least 6 emails received; exclude hard bounces at once and soft bounces after 4.
body: The agency builds rolling engagement segments and suppresses the rest to protect deliverability and cut ESP cost, since unengaged profiles are the ones most likely to mark mail as spam. Setup in Klaviyo: 1) Engaged segments for 30, 60, 90 and 120 days (optionally 7, 14, 180): can receive email AND (placed order, started checkout, added to cart, viewed product, active on site, opened or clicked email) at least once in the window. Site activity counts because those people are engaged with the brand even if not opening. 2) Unengaged 120 days: none of those events in 120 days AND received at least 6 emails in that window, so people who were never mailed are not misjudged (6 suits a three-campaigns-a-week schedule). 3) For a 365-day deep clean, use email metrics only and require about 12 received. 4) Send a sunset flow to the unengaged segment whose only goal is an open (biggest discount, curiosity subject lines), then suppress non-responders with 'suppress current members'. 5) Always exclude a marked-as-spam segment, hard bounces (one occurrence) and soft bounces (four occurrences) from campaigns. 6) Send most campaigns to engaged 90 days or tighter.

fails_when: Apple privacy opens inflate the opened metric, so some unengaged people look engaged; or very low send frequency, where 6 sends in 120 days is not reached and the threshold must be lowered.

claim: In Klaviyo, turn smart sending off on every flow but on for campaigns (16-hour window), and use a 5-day email attribution window excluding Apple privacy opens.
body: These are account-level defaults the agency applies before building anything. Smart sending skips anyone who received an email within a set window (16 hours is the agency's working default, editable in account settings). On campaigns it prevents back-to-back sends and over-mailing, so leave it on for nearly all campaigns. On flows it can silently skip a triggered message, such as a cart reminder or post-purchase email, because the person happened to get a campaign recently; those flow emails are often the highest-revenue sends, so switch it off on each flow email and enable UTM tracking at the same time. Attribution: keep email conversion attribution at 5 days after the last open or click, but choose the touchpoint setting that excludes Apple Mail privacy opens, because those auto-opens credit email with revenue it did not drive. SMS attribution is left at 1 day. Also enable anonymous visitor tracking so pre-identification browsing is back-filled when someone subscribes. Note that any attribution window inflates channel credit relative to incrementality; use holdouts if you need true lift.
conditions: Brands on Klaviyo; applies when setting up or auditing an account.
fails_when: Brands sending very frequent flows to the same people (several triggered flows overlapping) may need smart sending or flow filters on some flows to avoid over-mailing; attribution windows are a reporting choice, not a measure of incremental revenue.

claim: In abandon flows, hold any discount until about email 5 (day 4 to 5) with a real 48-hour expiry, then close with a plain-text founder email.
body: The agency's view is that offering a discount in the first or second abandon email trains shoppers to wait for one; after a few days without a code, many pay full price. Structure for cart and checkout abandonment: 1) Email 1 at 30 minutes to 2 hours: simple reminder of the items. 2) Emails 2 to 4, one day apart: reviews and social proof, objection handling (shipping, returns, sizing), specific USPs. 3) Email 5: first discount, framed with a 48-hour deadline. 4) Emails 6 and 7: either raise the discount if margins allow, or a plain-text email from the founder extending the same offer for 24 hours as a last chance. 5) Use unique (dynamic) codes so expiry is real; avoid static codes like WELCOME10. 6) Where checkout data shows a shipping charge, test free shipping instead of a percentage: on a 200 AOV, 10% costs at least 20, while free shipping may cost 10 and convert as well. 7) Watch spam complaint and unsubscribe rates; long flows of 14 to 20 emails exist but annoy. No lift figures are given.

fails_when: Brands whose shoppers already expect immediate codes (heavy-discount categories) may lose more carts by waiting; or no-discount brands, which should use the same slots for proof and objection handling only.

claim: Shorten the first-email delay the closer a flow sits to purchase: site abandon 1 to 4 hours, browse abandon 1 to 3, cart abandon 30 minutes to 2 hours.
body: The agency's flow timing ladder for Klaviyo, each to be A/B tested with a random 50% conditional split: 1) Site abandonment (active on site, no product view): first email after 1 to 4 hours; test 1 versus 4 hours. 2) Browse abandonment (viewed product): Klaviyo's default of 2 hours is a fair start; test 1 versus 3 hours. claim: Sign-up incentives under 10% rarely work; at AOV of about 200 or more, a fixed amount (20 off) usually beats the equal percentage (10% off).
body: The agency treats the offer as the single biggest driver of popup sign-up rate. Rules it gives: 1) Anything below 10% off is generally not enticing; 5% only works for very high-AOV products. 2) Express the incentive in whichever form shows the bigger number. At a 200 AOV, 10% and 20 off cost the same, but 20 reads as larger, so a fixed amount tends to win; below about 100 AOV, a percentage usually shows the bigger number. 3) Test other offer types: buy one get one, buy one get one at 50%, free gift over a threshold, free shipping, early access, subscription discount. 4) For SMS, add a second step after email capture and test three angles: the same offer, a better offer for SMS (15% after a 10% email offer), or a 'VIP club' with early access and private sales. 5) Headline the reward directly ('Unlock 10% off your first order') rather than 'Sign up', and test button text such as 'Reveal my discount'. Also show a 'didn't get it in 5 minutes? check spam' message to cut support tickets from new subscribers whose first email lands in spam. No conversion figures are given for these tests.

claim: Send replenishment reminders at about 75% of the usage cycle (8 to 15% conversion versus 1 to 3% for promos) and a second-purchase nudge 10 days post-delivery.
body: The playbook calls first-to-second purchase the highest-leverage retention move: the DTC average repeat rate is about 28.2% over 12 months, ranging from about 9.9% in luxury to 65.2% in grocery (vendor datasets), and roughly 70 to 81% of customers buy once in some datasets. Two timed plays: 1) Replenishment: for consumables, compute each product's usage cycle (units divided by daily use) and send a reorder reminder at about 75% of it, so it lands before the customer runs out. Reported conversion is 8 to 15% against 1 to 3% for general promotional emails. Cap at two messages per cycle. Offer subscription with easy skip, pause and cadence change, since rigid subscriptions drive cancellations and chargebacks. 2) Second-purchase nudge: about 10 days after the first order arrives, send relevant discovery (complementary products, the next step in the routine) with a modest 10 to 15% incentive; the playbook says 25 to 30% first-to-second conversion is achievable when done well. Measure 90-day repeat rate by cohort before and after. Benchmarks are vendor-sourced and vary widely by category.

body: Benchmarks the playbook cites from email platforms (flagged as vendor data, directionally consistent): automated win-back flows reactivate 12 to 20% of lapsed customers on average and 20 to 35% in the top quartile; emails sent 30 to 45 days after the last purchase convert about 2.3x better than those sent at 90 days or more (Klaviyo benchmark); escalating incentives (no discount, then 10%, then 15%, then free shipping) beat a flat discount by about 34% (Omnisend). claim: Send campaigns broad 80% of the time, keep at least 50% of the list engaged, and re-warm dormant subscribers by adding about 10% slices of them to each send.
body: Cowan argues against hyper-segmented campaigns: a 1,000-person segment gets real effort but little response, and only a few percent of a list (he says about 3%) is ready to buy on any given day. Make strong content and send it to as many people as deliverability allows about 80% of the time, keeping roughly 20% of sends for targeted goals (excess stock, VIP perks, at-risk champions). The agency split the 375,000 unengaged into 10 random groups of about 37,500 and added one group to each engaged send; with 20 to 30% opening, the engaged base grew send by send. After several months the brand mailed the whole list for Black Friday 2025 and beat the prior year by 40%. Track engaged-segment size as a goal.

claim: Split every flow first by new, returning and loyal or subscriber customers; under about $10-20M a year the usual retention constraint is first-to-second order conversion.
body: Angus Cowan's agency structures every Klaviyo flow (abandoned cart and checkout, browse, post-purchase, cross-sell) with a first split by customer stage: new (never bought; tackle trust and price, can be more aggressive with incentives), returning (skip the brand introduction, limited incentives) and loyal or subscriber (protect the relationship, ideally no incentive). Only after that split test product or cart-value splits; splitting by product first means a five-time buyer gets the same message as a stranger. The account is then read through three stages: acquisition, first-to-second order conversion (correlates with 90-day LTGP) and revenue from the top 20% of customers (correlates with 365-day LTGP). For most brands under about $10 to $20 million a year, the constraint is first-to-second order conversion; VIP work pays off later, when VIPs should drive 50% or more of revenue and about 80% of profit. claim: Programmatic direct mail triggered like an abandoned-cart email reports large vendor lifts: Lulu and Georgia 22x iROAS, Magazine.co.uk +38.8% conversions with one letter per 30 days.
body: Programmatic direct mail sends a printed postcard or letter automatically from the same behavioural triggers that fire emails (browse, cart abandonment), usually arriving within days and showing the exact products viewed. claim: Engineer four demand peaks a year, one per quarter, by owning a cultural moment beyond BFCM and Mother's Day; a reason to buy now lifts conversion at flat CPMs.
body: Most brands have two natural peaks: Black Friday/Cyber Monday and, for many categories, Mother's Day. Holiday's agency aims for four, one per quarter, because peaks balance cash flow through the year and keep the team in a rhythm. A peak is created by giving the customer a narrative reason to buy today, which raises conversion rate while ad costs (CPMs) stay roughly the same, so efficiency improves. The example is APL, the Los Angeles footwear brand: with Black Friday and Mother's Day already fixed, they looked for a March moment and built a campaign around International Women's Day, telling stories of customers and influencers and going all in on celebrating them, turning it into a moment the brand could own. Another client attached to Veterans Day. To apply: list each quarter's open months, choose a date or cause that genuinely fits the brand's customers, plan product (limited editions work well), creative, email and SMS around it, and avoid a generic sitewide discount as the only reason, which trains customers to wait for sales.

fails_when: The chosen moment does not fit the brand, which reads as opportunistic (cause marketing backlash); or the peak relies only on discounting, cutting margin and pulling demand forward rather than creating it.

claim: 'Email should be 50% of revenue' is not a benchmark: Klaviyo's default 5-day open window works like view-through, so attributed revenue mostly measures send aggressiveness, not incrementality.
body: Agencies sell email on targets such as 30% or 50% of store revenue attributed to Klaviyo. The guest, who runs an email agency, calls this the wrong scorecard. Klaviyo's default attribution credits a purchase to an email if the person opened it within five days or clicked within five days; the open window behaves much like a view-through metric, so a returning customer who was going to buy anyway gets credited to whichever email they glanced at. An agency paid on attributed revenue can raise it simply by sending more often to people about to purchase, which can hurt brand perception and list health. The figure also depends on business model: a supplement brand with frequent repeat orders will attribute far more than a furniture brand, regardless of email quality. Use it properly: because nearly every brand runs the default settings, attributed revenue is a fair trend line and a rough comparison point, and a rising number usually means emails are reaching buyers. For decisions, split attributed revenue into new versus returning customers (email's effect on returning buyers is far less incremental than it looks), and judge the program on repeat purchase rate, LTV and, where possible, holdout or lift tests.

fails_when: Attribution settings have been tightened (click-only, shorter windows) or holdout groups exist, in which case attributed revenue is closer to incremental; the critique is about using it as a target, not about tracking it.

claim: Minimum email test sizes: sign-up forms 3,000 to 5,000 impressions per variant over 15 days, flows 1,000 recipients per variant, campaigns a manual 50/50 split judged on revenue.
body: The agency's working floors for Klaviyo tests. Sign-up forms: at least 3,000 to 5,000 impressions per variant and at least 15 days of runtime, sometimes 7 days, even on high-traffic stores that hit the impressions in a day, because day-of-week effects need to wash out. Flows: at least 1,000 recipients per variant; 500 can be enough only when the gap between variants is very large. Campaigns: always a manual 50/50 split sent to the full audience, then analyse after a few days. Avoid the automatic option that sends 20% to A, 20% to B and the winner to the remaining 60% after a few hours: the majority gets the email at a worse time, and two to four hours is too short to call a winner. Judge on revenue (the deciding metric in the host's estimate of 95% of tests), not open or click rate; a 7 a.m. send may win opens while a 2 p.m. send wins revenue. Put subject-line and sender-name tests last: they are easy but move little. Higher-value tests: offer, angle or pain point, landing page destination, and dynamic product blocks. Keep tests running in sequence so learning compounds.

fails_when: Small lists and low-traffic stores that cannot reach the floors, where tests should be larger changes run longer or skipped; revenue-per-recipient comparisons skewed by one large order; these floors are rules of thumb, not power calculations.

claim: Most second purchases happen within 30 days of the first; send the post-purchase thank-you with a cross-sell about 10 minutes after the order, then a reassurance email 2 days later.
body: In the agency's client data (first-to-second purchase rate and time between orders), most repeat purchases happen within 30 days of the first order, so the post-purchase flow is the main window to lift second-order rate. It also reduces returns by countering buyer's remorse. Build: trigger on placed order, wait about 10 minutes rather than sending instantly (the store's transactional confirmation and shipping emails already go out), then send a thank-you with the key information and a cross-sell; the host says even a plain link back to the site gets a good placed-order rate from this email. About two days later, send an 'order on its way' email that builds excitement, restates the value of what they bought and cross-sells again, timed to your shipping speed. Split new customers (placed order = 1) from returning customers so the content and offers fit. Turn smart sending off on every email in the flow, or buyers who bought from a campaign in the last hours will be skipped. claim: Tell best customers about a real coming shortage as exclusive news: in Cialdini's beef study, scarcity news doubled orders and scarcity framed as insider news sextupled them.
body: A beef importer's sales staff phoned their usual trade buyers three ways: a standard pitch; the standard pitch plus news that imported beef would be in short supply in coming months; and the same scarcity news presented as information from the company's exclusive contacts, not generally available. Buyers told about the coming shortage ordered more than twice as much as the standard group. Buyers who heard it as exclusive news ordered six times as much. Both the product and the information about it were scarce, and each added persuasive weight. Store application: when you genuinely face a constraint (a supplier price rise, a discontinued colourway, a harvest shortfall, a final production run), tell your VIP or repeat-customer segment first, by email or SMS, before announcing publicly, and say plainly that they are hearing it ahead of everyone else and why. Give a specific window before the general announcement. Measure order rate and units per order against a segment that gets the news at the public launch. Use it sparingly; if every email claims insider news, it stops being scarce information.

fails_when: The shortage is invented or exaggerated, which risks consumer-protection complaints and burns the list's trust; and categories where buyers cannot stock up (perishables, single-use purchases) gain less from early notice.

claim: US CAN-SPAM: subject lines must not deceive, marketing email must be identified as an ad, carry a valid postal address and an opt-out honoured within 10 business days.
body: A mixed order and promo email is commercial if its subject reads commercial. The FTC's compliance guide sets out the rules for commercial email to US recipients. Header information must be accurate and identify the sender. The subject line must not be deceptive and must match the content. The message must be clearly identified as an advertisement, include a valid physical postal address (a street address, registered post office box or registered private mailbox), and offer a clear way to stop marketing email, which must keep working for at least 30 days after sending. Opt-outs must be honoured within 10 business days, with no fee and no information asked beyond the email address. The primary purpose decides which rules apply: purely transactional or relationship messages are largely exempt, but a mixed message counts as commercial if a reasonable reader would see the subject line as commercial or if the transactional content is not mainly at the start. A promotional message must give the recipient an opt-out in the same message, and if promotional content is mixed into a transactional or service message, the whole message is treated as promotional and goes only to people who have not blocked that category or who consented. Messages with URLs, APKs, OTT links or callback numbers are scrubbed against the sender's whitelist. claim: CAN-SPAM makes no exception for business-to-business email: sales emails to shops need accurate headers, honest subject lines, a postal address and an opt-out honoured within 10 business days; penalties reach 53,088 dollars per email.
body: The FTC's compliance guide says the law makes no exception for business-to-business email. A commercial message must have accurate From, To, Reply-To and routing information; a subject line that reflects the content; a clear disclosure that it is an advertisement; a valid physical postal address; and a clear, easy way to opt out of future marketing email, with opt-outs honoured within 10 business days. Each separate email that breaks the law can draw a penalty of up to 53,088 dollars. How to use it: every pitch and follow-up to a US retailer, boutique or corporate buyer carries the brand's postal address and a plain line such as 'Reply stop and I will not email again', and a stop ends the sequence for that address at once.
conditions: Commercial email to US recipients, as stated in the FTC guide on the date fetched.
fails_when: The message is purely transactional or relationship content (for example an invoice for an agreed order), which has different rules.
